findings.title: Dynamic Zod keys collapse and strip token fields
findings.body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` in `minimumTokenResponseSchema` both evaluate to the same static key such as `[object Object]`, so the schema is effectively only `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": ... }`. It does not validate any numeric expiry field as the comment claims, and because `z.object` strips unknown fields, every other field returned by the sync endpoint (`expiry_date`, `expires_in`, `refresh_token`, etc.) is discarded. In sync mode callers persist incomplete tokens.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is overwritten with the literal string `refresh_token`
findings.body: When the provider or sync endpoint does not return a new refresh token, this code writes the literal value `"refresh_token"` into the parsed data. For O365, where `refresh_token` is optional in the schema, this replaces the existing valid refresh token during the merge in `Office365CalendarService`, so the next refresh fails. It also guarantees corruption in sync mode for any callers that store `refresh_token`.

findings.title: Google Calendar stores the safeParse wrapper instead of credential data
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a `SafeParseReturnType` object (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data itself. Assigning it to `key` and then writing `key` to `prisma.credential.update` changes the database credential to `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. On the next use, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` no longer sees top-level `access_token`, so Google Calendar stops working after the first token refresh. The code should store `parsed.data` or the helper should return data consistently.

findings.title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response but callers expect token objects
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` from `fetch`. Several callers assume provider-specific objects instead: `GoogleCalendarService` reads `res?.data`, `HubspotCalendarService` treats it as a `HubspotToken` and mutates `expiresIn`, and Zoho Bigin/CRM read `tokenInfo.data.error`. These paths throw TypeErrors or persist invalid credentials whenever sync is enabled. The helper needs a consistent parsed contract, or each caller must explicitly handle `Response`.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sends credential ID as calcomUserId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the third argument to be the Cal.com user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint. `BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken` passes `credentialId`, which is the internal `Credential` primary key, not `credential.userId`. The parent app will look up the wrong user and may return tokens for a different user, which are then written to this credential.

findings.title: Synced credentials do not clear the invalid flag
findings.body: When an existing credential is found, the webhook only updates `key`. If the credential had been marked invalid (Google, Webex, Zoom, etc.), it remains invalid after fresh credentials are synced, so Cal.com continues to reject the newly provided valid credentials. The update should also reset `invalid` to false when new keys are supplied.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the credential sync endpoint
findings.body: The new Salesforce refresh path calls `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. With `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured, Salesforce never asks the parent application to refresh, so the credential-sync feature does not apply to Salesforce and self-hosters relying on the parent app as source of truth still depend on local Salesforce secrets. It should use the same sync helper as the other apps or document that Salesforce is unsupported.

findings.title: No tests cover the new credential-sync endpoint or refresh helpers
findings.body: This PR adds a security-sensitive webhook and rewrites token refresh behavior across multiple apps without tests. Basic tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, the sync-enabled `refreshOAuthTokens` path, and the webhook update/create flow would have caught the malformed Zod schema, literal `refresh_token` injection, wrong user ID, and raw `Response` handling issues.
